optical-materials-001.question: Which statement correctly describes how the refractive index of an optical glass that is transparent in the visible changes with wavelength?
choices: The index increases as the wavelength gets longer, so in a prism red light is bent more than blue light
The index decreases as the wavelength gets longer, and the change becomes steeper at shorter wavelengths, closer to the ultraviolet absorption
In the transparent range the index is constant regardless of wavelength; it changes only at wavelengths where there is absorption
optical-materials-001.explanation: In its transparent range a material shows normal dispersion: the longer the wavelength, the lower the refractive index. A BK7-type glass, for example, has about 1.522 at the F line (486.1 nm) and about 1.514 at the C line (656.3 nm). The change becomes steeper as the ultraviolet absorption band is approached, so the magnitude of dn/dλ grows at shorter wavelengths. As a result, blue light is bent more in a prism, and the option saying red is bent more has it backwards. The index varies with wavelength even in the transparent range, so the option claiming it is constant is also wrong; this variation is what causes chromatic aberration in a single lens. Inside an absorption band, anomalous dispersion occurs, where the index rises with wavelength.

optical-materials-002.question: A glass has refractive indices nd = 1.5168 at the d line (587.6 nm), nF = 1.52238 at the F line (486.1 nm) and nC = 1.51432 at the C line (656.3 nm). Which combination of the Abbe number Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC) and the classification of this glass is correct? (As a guide, glasses with an Abbe number above about 50 are called crown glasses and those below, flint glasses.)
choices: About 64, classified as a crown glass
About 64, classified as a flint glass
About 0.016, classified as a high-dispersion glass
optical-materials-002.explanation: Since nF − nC = 1.52238 − 1.51432 = 0.00806, Vd = 0.5168/0.00806 ≈ 64.1. The Abbe number expresses how small the dispersion is: the larger the value, the smaller the difference in index between wavelengths. About 64 is above the guide value of 50, so this is a low-dispersion crown glass (a typical value for BK7-type glass). The flint option comes from remembering it backwards, as if a larger Abbe number meant larger dispersion. About 0.016 is (nF − nC)/(nd − 1), with numerator and denominator swapped, and is not the Abbe number. Achromatic lenses are made by combining a positive lens of high-Abbe-number crown with a negative lens of low-Abbe-number flint.

optical-materials-003.question: Which statement correctly describes the idea behind the Sellmeier equation n²(λ) = 1 + Σ Bᵢλ²/(λ² − Cᵢ), which expresses the wavelength dispersion of the refractive index?
choices: It is merely a polynomial fitted to measured values, with no physical meaning in its terms, so it can be used with good accuracy as is even outside the measured wavelength range
It is an equation for the temperature dependence of the index, with Cᵢ corresponding to thermal expansion and Bᵢ to the thermo-optic coefficient dn/dT
It treats the electrons and lattice vibrations as oscillators resonant at wavelengths √Cᵢ, and the transparent range lies between the ultraviolet and infrared resonances
optical-materials-003.explanation: The Sellmeier equation represents electronic polarization (ultraviolet resonances) and lattice vibrations (infrared resonances) as oscillators, and each term diverges at its resonance wavelength √Cᵢ. With typical coefficients for fused silica, the resonances lie in the ultraviolet at about 0.068 µm and 0.116 µm and in the infrared at about 9.9 µm, and normal dispersion appears in the transparent range between them. The index changes more steeply at shorter wavelengths because the ultraviolet resonances are being approached. The option describing a polynomial with no physical meaning is closer to empirical formulas such as Cauchy's equation, and neither kind of formula is guaranteed to be accurate outside the measured range or inside absorption bands. The temperature dependence is handled separately as the thermo-optic coefficient dn/dT, and Cᵢ is not a thermal expansion coefficient.

optical-materials-004.question: Fused silica has a refractive index n = 1.444 at a wavelength of 1.55 µm and a wavelength derivative of the index dn/dλ = −0.0118 µm⁻¹. Which value is closest to the group index ng = n − λ dn/dλ at this wavelength?
choices: About 1.426
About 1.444
About 1.462
optical-materials-004.explanation: ng = n − λ dn/dλ = 1.444 − 1.55 × (−0.0118) = 1.444 + 0.0183 ≈ 1.462. With normal dispersion dn/dλ < 0, so the group index is larger than the refractive index, and the envelope of a pulse or modulation travels at c/ng ≈ 2.05×10⁸ m/s, slower than c/n. About 1.426 reverses the sign of dn/dλ; in a material with normal dispersion, ng < n never happens. About 1.444 is the refractive index itself, which sets the phase velocity, and does not distinguish it from the group index. When finding distances with an OTDR or estimating pulse arrival times, use the group index rather than the refractive index. The wavelength dependence of the group index is what gives the material dispersion of a fiber.

optical-materials-005.question: Which window material is best suited to transmit, in a single piece, from 0.25 µm in the ultraviolet to 8 µm in the infrared? (Assume a thickness of a few mm and ignore reflection losses at the surfaces.)
choices: Calcium fluoride (CaF₂) crystal
Sapphire (Al₂O₃) crystal
Fused silica (SiO₂) glass
optical-materials-005.explanation: The short-wavelength edge of the transmission range is set by band-gap absorption and the long-wavelength edge by multiphonon absorption of lattice vibrations. CaF₂ has a large band gap of about 12 eV and is a fluoride with weak bonds and heavy atoms, so it transmits from about 0.13 µm to around 10 µm and covers 0.25–8 µm in one piece. Sapphire transmits from around 0.2 µm, but in the infrared its absorption becomes strong at about 5 µm. Fused silica transmits into the deep ultraviolet, but its infrared limit is about 3.5 µm. Oxides have strong bonds and light atoms, so their infrared edge is shorter than that of fluorides. CaF₂ is sensitive to thermal shock and cracks easily, so sudden temperature changes should be avoided when handling it.

optical-materials-006.question: Depending on how it is made, synthetic fused silica either contains many OH groups (around several hundred to 1000 ppm) or almost none. Which application is the most appropriate one for choosing low-OH synthetic fused silica?
choices: Applications where deep-ultraviolet transmission and durability matter most, such as the optics of 193 nm ArF excimer lasers
Applications transmitting near- to mid-infrared light, including wavelengths around 2.7 µm
Visible lenses where the wavelength dispersion should be made small
optical-materials-006.explanation: OH groups in silica have a strong absorption at about 2.7 µm from the fundamental stretching vibration, and absorptions from its overtones and combination bands at about 1.38 µm and 2.2 µm. So windows and lenses that pass infrared light including the region around 2.7 µm use infrared-grade silica with almost no OH. The "water peak", the higher loss around 1.38 µm in optical fibers, has the same cause. For deep-ultraviolet excimer lasers, high-OH synthetic silica, with excellent ultraviolet transmission and resistance to laser-induced degradation, is generally used, so the option naming ArF excimer-laser optics has it backwards. The OH content hardly changes the visible dispersion, so to reduce dispersion you would choose a material with a large Abbe number.

optical-materials-007.question: Sapphire (Al₂O₃) is a uniaxial crystal with a small birefringence (|ne − no| ≈ 0.008). Which way of cutting it is correct for a window that passes normally incident light without changing its polarization state?
choices: Make the c axis (optic axis) perpendicular to the window face (a c-plane cut), so that light travels parallel to the c axis
Cutting with the c axis lying in the plane of the window gives no birefringence for any polarization

Regardless of crystal orientation, choosing a thickness at which the phase difference between the two polarizations is an integer number of wavelengths leaves the polarization unchanged at every wavelength
optical-materials-007.explanation: In a uniaxial crystal, light traveling parallel to the optic axis sees the ordinary index no for any polarization direction, so no phase difference from birefringence arises. Windows meant to preserve polarization therefore use c-plane substrates with the c axis perpendicular to the face. With the c axis in the plane, birefringence acts at its largest: even at 1 mm thickness the path difference is about 0.008 mm, a dozen or so wavelengths of 633 nm light, and the window acts as a wave plate. Matching the phase difference to an integer number of wavelengths works only at a particular wavelength and temperature, so that option is wrong. Even c-plane windows show some birefringence for oblique incidence or focused light, so in polarization-sensitive optics the angle of incidence also needs attention.

optical-materials-008.question: A dielectric multilayer mirror is made on a glass substrate (ns = 1.52) by alternately stacking λ/4 layers of high index nH = 2.35 and low index nL = 1.45 into the 11-layer structure (HL)⁵H (with high-index layers at both ends). Which value is closest to the reflectance at the design wavelength for light normally incident from the air side? Take the reflectance of this structure as R = [(1 − Y)/(1 + Y)]², Y = (nH/nL)^(2N)·nH²/ns (N = 5).
choices: About 90.6%
About 32%
About 99.1%
optical-materials-008.explanation: nH/nL = 2.35/1.45 ≈ 1.621, so (nH/nL)¹⁰ ≈ 125.0, and nH²/ns = 5.5225/1.52 ≈ 3.633, giving Y ≈ 454. R = [(1 − 454)/(1 + 454)]² ≈ (0.9956)² ≈ 0.991, or about 99.1%. About 90.6% uses an exponent of N instead of 2N, missing that both the high-to-low and low-to-high boundaries of each pair contribute to the reflection. About 32% is the reflectance of a single high-index layer (Y = nH²/ns). Each additional pair multiplies Y by (nH/nL)² ≈ 2.6, and the reflectance approaches 100%. Because a higher reflectance than a metal mirror can be obtained with absorption-free dielectrics alone, such mirrors are used in laser resonators.

optical-materials-009.question: For a λ/4-stack dielectric multilayer mirror, which method correctly widens the range of wavelengths over which high reflectance is obtained (the high-reflectance band), measured relative to the center wavelength as Δλ/λ₀?
choices: Increase the number of pairs
Increase the index difference between the high-index and low-index layers
Make all the layers thicker by the same proportion
optical-materials-009.explanation: The relative width of the high-reflectance band of a λ/4 stack is Δλ/λ₀ ≈ (4/π) arcsin[(nH − nL)/(nH + nL)], set only by the ratio of the indices of the two materials. It is about 0.30 for TiO₂ (2.35) with SiO₂ (1.45) and about 0.23 for Ta₂O₅ (2.1) with SiO₂, so the larger the index difference, the wider the band. Adding pairs raises the reflectance within the band and sharpens its edges, but barely changes its width. Making all layers thicker by the same proportion only moves the band center to longer wavelengths and scales the width in proportion to the center wavelength, so Δλ/λ₀ stays the same. To widen it further, stacks with shifted center wavelengths are combined.

optical-materials-010.question: Light at 532 nm is normally incident on a λ/4-stack high-reflectance mirror designed for λ₀ = 1064 nm (each layer having an optical thickness of λ₀/4). Ignoring material dispersion, which statement correctly describes the mirror's reflection at 532 nm?
choices: Because 532 nm is the second harmonic of 1064 nm, the reflectance is high, just as in the high-reflection band at the design wavelength
Each layer becomes optically a half wave thick and acts as if absent, so the reflectance is as low as that of the bare substrate
Since 532 nm is exactly half of λ₀, the reflectance also falls to about half of its value at the design wavelength, that is, about 50%
optical-materials-010.explanation: The optical thickness of each layer, λ₀/4 = 266 nm, is a half wave for 532 nm light. At that wavelength a half-wave layer has a characteristic matrix equal to the identity (apart from sign) and acts as an "absentee layer" that makes no difference whether present or not. The whole stack therefore behaves as if it had vanished, and the reflectance drops to roughly the 4% of the glass substrate (1.52) alone. High reflectance returns at wavelengths where each layer is an odd multiple of λ/4, such as λ₀/3 (about 355 nm) and λ₀/5. The option claiming high reflectance as at the design wavelength misses that this happens only at these odd orders. Nor is there a proportional relation in which halving the wavelength halves the reflectance. Mirrors that reflect both 1064 nm and 532 nm use designs that depart from λ/4.

optical-materials-011.question: Which statement correctly describes what happens when a dielectric multilayer narrow-bandpass filter is tilted away from normal incidence?
choices: The center of the passband shifts to shorter wavelengths, and at large tilts the characteristics split between s- and p-polarization
The center of the passband shifts to longer wavelengths because the optical path in the layers grows, and no difference arises between polarizations
The physical thickness of the layers does not change, so the center wavelength stays the same and only the passband width broadens slightly
optical-materials-011.explanation: For light traveling obliquely in the films, the phase thickness of each layer becomes 2πnd cosθ/λ (θ is the angle inside the film), so the layers act as if thinner by the factor cosθ. The center wavelength therefore shifts to shorter wavelengths, as λ(θ) ≈ λ₀√(1 − (sinθ/n_eff)²). Tilting a filter with an effective index n_eff = 1.8 and a design wavelength of 1550 nm by 30° moves it to about 1489 nm. The option with a shift to longer wavelengths has the direction backwards. At oblique incidence the effective film indices differ for s- and p-polarization, so at large angles the characteristics split by polarization. The option saying the center wavelength does not change is also wrong; this property can be put to use to tune the transmitted wavelength by tilting the filter.

optical-materials-012.question: Compare the elongation of a 100 mm long part when its temperature rises by 10 K, for a BK7-type optical glass (linear expansion coefficient 7.1×10⁻⁶ /K) and for fused silica (0.55×10⁻⁶ /K). Which combination of elongations is correct?
choices: About 71 µm for BK7-type glass and about 5.5 µm for fused silica
About 0.71 µm for BK7-type glass and about 0.055 µm for fused silica
About 7.1 µm for BK7-type glass and about 0.55 µm for fused silica
optical-materials-012.explanation: The elongation is ΔL = αLΔT. For BK7-type glass it is 7.1×10⁻⁶ × 100 mm × 10 = 7.1×10⁻³ mm = 7.1 µm, and for fused silica 0.55×10⁻⁶ × 100 mm × 10 = 0.55 µm. About 71 µm and about 0.71 µm are off by a factor of ten in converting between mm and µm. 7.1 µm is about 11 times the 633 nm wavelength, a change that cannot be ignored in interferometers and resonators. Fused silica expands about 13 times less and also resists thermal shock, so it is used for precision substrates and ultraviolet optics. Telescope primary mirrors and reference cavities use glass-ceramics or low-expansion glasses tuned for nearly zero expansion. The temperature coefficient of the index, dn/dT, also adds to temperature-induced changes in optical path.

optical-materials-013.question: An anti-reflection coating is specified to have a laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT) of 10 J/cm² at a wavelength of 1064 nm and a pulse width of 10 ns. Using the rule of thumb that, in the range of about 1 ns to 100 ns, the threshold fluence scales with the square root of the pulse width, which value is closest to the threshold at the same wavelength for a pulse width of 1 ns?
choices: About 3.2 J/cm²
About 1.0 J/cm²
About 32 J/cm²
optical-materials-013.explanation: The rule of thumb is F(τ₂) = F(τ₁)√(τ₂/τ₁), giving 10 J/cm² × √(1/10) ≈ 3.2 J/cm². For ns pulses, the distance over which heat generated at defects or by absorption in the film diffuses scales as √(Dτ), so shorter pulses let heat escape less and damage occurs at lower fluence. About 1.0 J/cm² scales the threshold in proportion to the pulse width, which amounts to assuming the same peak intensity. About 32 J/cm² inverts the square-root scaling, so that shorter pulses would cause less damage. This rule of thumb is empirical for the range where heating is the main cause; at ps to fs, different mechanisms such as multiphoton absorption take over, so it cannot be extrapolated. The threshold also depends on wavelength, so in practice check the value for the conditions of use and design with a margin.

optical-materials-014.question: What is the main reason calcite or YVO₄, rather than crystal quartz, is often used as the material for Glan–Taylor polarizers and beam displacers (elements that split light by polarization into two parallel beams)?
choices: Calcite and YVO₄ are isotropic crystals with no birefringence, so polarizations are separated purely by the difference between total internal and Fresnel reflection at the oblique face between the two prisms
Their birefringence |ne − no| is more than ten times that of quartz (about 0.009), so a short crystal can widely separate the angles or positions of the two polarizations

They are transparent over a wider range from ultraviolet to infrared than quartz, and their optical rotation, larger than that of quartz, turns the polarization plane by a large angle within a short crystal
optical-materials-014.explanation: In elements that separate polarizations, the larger the index difference between the two polarizations, the larger the difference in total-internal-reflection conditions and propagation directions. The birefringence of calcite is about 0.17 in the visible and that of YVO₄ about 0.2, more than ten times quartz's roughly 0.009, which makes possible Glan–Taylor polarizers that remove one polarization by total internal reflection at an air gap, and beam displacers that separate two beams within a length of a few mm. The option claiming no birefringence has it backwards; birefringence is the very principle of these elements. The option citing transmission range and optical rotation is also wrong: crystal quartz transmits from about 0.15 µm in the ultraviolet and has a wider range than calcite, while calcite and YVO₄ are centrosymmetric crystals and show no optical rotation. Quartz's small birefringence is instead put to use in wave plates of manageable thickness.

optical-materials-015.question: A glass plate with a photoelastic (stress-optic) coefficient K = 2.8×10⁻¹² Pa⁻¹ is under a uniaxial stress of 2 MPa perpendicular to the direction of light propagation. Which value is closest to the optical path difference Δ = Kσd between the two polarizations for light passing through a thickness of 20 mm?
choices: About 11 nm
About 1.1 µm
About 112 nm
optical-materials-015.explanation: Δ = Kσd = 2.8×10⁻¹² Pa⁻¹ × 2×10⁶ Pa × 0.020 m = 1.12×10⁻⁷ m ≈ 112 nm. This is about 0.18 of a 633 nm wavelength, about 70% of a quarter wave (about 158 nm), so linearly polarized light clearly turns elliptical. About 11 nm is the value calculated with a thickness of 2 mm, and about 1.1 µm is off by a factor of ten in the other direction. Even an isotropic glass, when stressed, has different indices along and perpendicular to the stress direction, giving stress birefringence. Glass specifications express birefringence from residual stress as the optical path difference per centimeter of thickness (nm/cm). This example corresponds to 56 nm/cm, so precision optics that use polarization choose well-annealed glass and avoid overtightening the mounts.

optical-materials-016.question: A colored glass filter has an internal transmittance (transmittance due to absorption in the material alone, excluding surface reflections) of 80% at a thickness of 10 mm. Which value is closest to the internal transmittance of the same material at a thickness of 30 mm? Assume the absorption follows the Beer-Lambert law.
choices: About 40%
About 51%
About 93%
optical-materials-016.explanation: The transmittance due to absorption is T = exp(−αd), falling exponentially with thickness. Tripling the thickness gives T₃₀ = (T₁₀)³ = 0.80³ = 0.512, about 51%. About 40% assumes that losing 20% in 10 mm means losing 60% in 30 mm, a proportional estimate valid only for weak absorption. About 93% is the cube root of 0.80, using the thickness ratio the wrong way round. Glass catalogs give internal transmittance at thicknesses such as 10 mm or 25 mm, and other thicknesses are converted using this exponential relation. The actual filter transmittance is this value multiplied by the reflection losses at both faces (about 4% per face for an index of 1.5).

optical-materials-017.question: You want a metal mirror with high reflectance over a broad range from the ultraviolet at 200–400 nm through the visible. Which metal is the most suitable to deposit?
choices: Aluminum. Its reflectance is about 85–90% from the ultraviolet through the visible, and it is used with a protective overcoat such as MgF₂ to prevent oxidation
Silver. It has the highest visible reflectance of any metal, and that reflectance stays at the same 95% or more all the way down to short ultraviolet wavelengths
Gold. Its infrared reflectance is high and it is chemically stable and does not oxidize, so even without an overcoat it reflects about 98% in the ultraviolet and blue
optical-materials-017.explanation: A metal reflects strongly at frequencies below the frequency up to which its free electrons can follow the field (the plasma frequency). Aluminum has a high plasma frequency and reflects about 85–90% or more from about 200 nm in the ultraviolet through the visible and infrared (with a small dip near 800 nm). Its surface oxidizes quickly, degrading the UV reflectance, so a thin protective layer such as MgF₂ is added. Silver exceeds 95% in the visible and infrared, but its reflectance drops sharply near 320 nm, making it unsuitable for the UV. Gold reaches about 98% in the infrared, but interband absorption makes its reflectance fall below about 600 nm, to around 40% in the blue, which is why it looks yellow.

optical-materials-018.question: Which combination correctly gives the most common lens material for a thermal camera operating in the long-wave infrared at 8–14 µm, together with a point to watch when using it?
choices: Fused silica. It is transparent from the ultraviolet to the long-wave infrared and its index is only about 1.45, so even without a coating each surface reflects only about 3%
Sapphire. It is hard, scratch-resistant and transparent into the long-wave infrared, but it is birefringent, so it must be cut with its c axis along the optical axis
Germanium. Its refractive index is about 4, so each surface reflects about 36% and an antireflection coating is essential; its absorption also rises at high temperature
optical-materials-018.explanation: Germanium transmits from about 2 to 14 µm and has a large index of about 4.0, giving strong refracting power even with gently curved surfaces. Its normal-incidence reflectance is ((4.0 − 1)/(4.0 + 1))² = 0.36 (36%), so two surfaces would lose more than half the light, and an antireflection coating is essential. As the temperature rises, absorption by thermally generated free carriers increases, and transmission drops above roughly 100 °C. Fused silica absorbs beyond about 4 µm because of Si–O lattice vibrations, and sapphire absorbs from around 5 µm onward, so neither can be used at 8–14 µm. Other materials used in this band include ZnSe and chalcogenide glasses.

optical-materials-019.question: A laser pulse of energy 10 mJ strikes an optical component with a Gaussian distribution F(r) = F₀ exp(−2r²/w²) and beam radius w = 0.5 mm (the radius where the intensity falls to 1/e² of the center). Which value is closest to the fluence F₀ at the beam center?
choices: About 1.3 J/cm²
About 2.5 J/cm²
About 5.1 J/cm²
optical-materials-019.explanation: Integrating F(r) = F₀ exp(−2r²/w²) over the whole plane gives E = F₀πw²/2, so F₀ = 2E/(πw²). With w = 0.05 cm, πw² ≈ 7.85×10⁻³ cm², so F₀ = 2 × 0.010 J / 7.85×10⁻³ cm² ≈ 2.5 J/cm². About 1.3 J/cm² is the average obtained by dividing the energy by the area of a circle of radius w; at the center of a Gaussian beam the fluence is twice that. About 5.1 J/cm² wrongly treats w as a diameter and divides by a circle of radius w/2. Damage starts at the most intense point, the center, so the damage threshold should be compared with the peak fluence, and the definition of the beam size (1/e² or FWHM) must be checked.

optical-materials-020.question: Glass-ceramics with a linear expansion coefficient of almost zero near room temperature (of order 10⁻⁸ /K) are used as substrates for large telescope mirrors and precision metrology references. Which statement correctly describes how the expansion is made almost zero?
choices: Fine crystals with negative expansion, precipitated by heat treatment, are balanced in proportion against the remaining glass with positive expansion, so the two cancel
Crystals are eliminated entirely to make the atomic arrangement disordered, so the atomic spacing does not change with temperature and the expansion is zero at every temperature
Large amounts of high-index heavy-metal oxides are added to strengthen the atomic bonds, suppressing thermal vibration so that the expansion becomes almost zero
optical-materials-020.explanation: Heat-treating a lithium aluminosilicate glass precipitates fine crystals with a structure similar to high-temperature quartz. These crystals have negative expansion, shrinking as temperature rises, and matching their volume fraction to the remaining glass, which expands positively, brings the expansion near room temperature to almost zero. When the crystals are much smaller than the wavelength of light, the material can even be transparent in the visible. Fused silica doped with a few percent TiO₂ is another low-expansion material. Being amorphous does not remove expansion: amorphous fused silica still expands by about 0.55×10⁻⁶ /K. Additives that strengthen bonds cannot by themselves make the expansion zero; near-zero expansion comes from cancellation between positive and negative contributions.

optical-materials-021.question: A fused-silica window 10 mm thick (refractive index n = 1.45, thermo-optic coefficient dn/dT = 1.0×10⁻⁵ /K, linear expansion coefficient α = 0.55×10⁻⁶ /K) warms by 10 K. Taking the change of the optical path nL through the window as Δ(nL) = L(dn/dT + nα)ΔT, which value is closest?
choices: About 0.08 µm
About 11 µm
About 1.1 µm
optical-materials-021.explanation: dn/dT + nα = 1.0×10⁻⁵ + 1.45 × 0.55×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.08×10⁻⁵ /K, so Δ(nL) = 10 mm × 1.08×10⁻⁵ × 10 ≈ 1.08×10⁻³ mm, about 1.1 µm. About 0.08 µm uses only the expansion term nα and misses that, in fused silica, the index change contributes more than ten times as much. About 11 µm comes from a slip in converting mm to µm. 1.1 µm is about 1.7 times the 633 nm wavelength, so in interferometer windows and intracavity laser components, temperature gradients turn directly into wavefront distortion (thermal lensing). Even in low-expansion fused silica, the thermo-optic coefficient dominates optical-path stability.

optical-materials-022.question: Even as polycrystalline ceramics sintered from powder, YAG (Y₃Al₅O₁₂) and spinel (MgAl₂O₄) can be made transparent, whereas sintered alumina (Al₂O₃) tends to look milky white. Which is the main reason for this difference?
choices: YAG and spinel are cubic with no birefringence, but alumina is birefringent, so the index changes at each boundary between differently oriented grains and light scatters
Alumina has a small band gap and strongly absorbs the short-wavelength side of visible light, so light weakens inside the ceramic and only light scattered at the surface looks white
When sintered, the grains of YAG and spinel merge into one large single crystal with no grain boundaries, whereas alumina stays a polycrystal of small grains
optical-materials-022.explanation: In a polycrystal, light crosses many boundaries between randomly oriented grains. Cubic YAG and spinel are optically isotropic, with the same index for every grain orientation, so once pores and impurities are removed the boundaries do not scatter and the ceramic can be as clear as glass. Alumina (the same crystal as sapphire) is birefringent (about 0.008), so the index changes slightly at each boundary between differently oriented grains, and the accumulated scattering makes it milky. Alumina's band gap is large, about 9 eV, and it does not absorb visible light, so the whiteness is scattering, not absorption. Transparent ceramics remain polycrystalline; they do not become single crystals.

optical-materials-023.question: When optical glass is exposed for a long time to ionizing radiation (such as gamma rays) or intense ultraviolet light, it can turn brown and lose transmission at the short-wavelength end of the visible. Which combination of cause and remedy is correct?
choices: Organic contamination on the surface is burned by the radiation into a carbon film; repolishing and then cleaning the surface fully restores the transmission
Electrons and holes created by the radiation are trapped at defects in the glass to form color centers with absorption bands; cerium-doped radiation-resistant glass suppresses this
Radiation raises the density and refractive index of the glass, increasing surface reflectance; a thicker anti-reflection coating compensates for the added reflection
optical-materials-023.explanation: Radiation and UV light create electrons and holes in the glass. When they are trapped at defects such as oxygen vacancies, they form color centers with absorption bands in the visible and UV, so absorption grows from the short-wavelength side and the glass looks brown. In cerium-doped glass, Ce³⁺ and Ce⁴⁺ capture the electrons and holes first and suppress color-center formation, so such glass is used in optics for nuclear facilities and space. Color centers form inside the glass, so repolishing does not remove them (heating anneals some out). An increase in reflectance cannot explain the brown color or the wavelength-dependent absorption.

optical-materials-024.question: Which statement correctly compares injection-molded plastic lenses, such as PMMA (acrylic), with optical-glass lenses?
choices: Both the thermo-optic coefficient and thermal expansion are smaller than in glass, so focus barely shifts with temperature, making them suited to precision measurement optics
Stress birefringence from molding appears less than in glass, so they are easy to use as is in polarization optics and interferometers

Aspheres can be molded cheaply in volume, but the thermo-optic coefficient is one to two orders of magnitude larger than in glass (and negative) and expansion is also large, so focus shifts easily with temperature
optical-materials-024.explanation: Plastic is poured into a mold and solidified, so even aspheric lenses can be made cheaply in volume without polishing each one, and they are light and hard to break, which is why they are widely used in camera modules and lighting. However, PMMA has dn/dT of about −1×10⁻⁴ /K, one to two orders of magnitude larger than most optical glasses (around 10⁻⁶ /K), and a linear expansion coefficient of about 7×10⁻⁵ /K, about ten times that of glass, so the focal length shifts easily with temperature. Saying they resist temperature change is backwards. Flow orientation and uneven cooling during molding leave stress birefringence, which needs care in polarization optics. Water absorption can also change the index and shape.

optical-materials-025.question: When optical glasses are plotted with refractive index nd and Abbe number Vd as axes (the Abbe diagram), which combination of the general trend and the position of lanthanum-oxide glasses is correct?
choices: Index and Abbe number are unrelated and scatter evenly over the diagram; lanthanum glasses, like lead-containing flints, have low index and high dispersion and are used for the negative element of achromats
Higher-index glasses tend to have higher dispersion (lower Abbe number), but lanthanum glasses have a higher index at the same Abbe number, allowing gentler curvatures and less aberration
Higher-index glasses tend to have larger Abbe numbers and lower dispersion; lanthanum glasses lower the index to make the Abbe number even larger and are used for ultraviolet transmission
optical-materials-025.explanation: The refractive index is set by the ultraviolet absorption resonances, and glasses whose resonances lie closer to the visible (at longer wavelengths) have a higher index and also more dispersion in the visible. So on the Abbe diagram, higher-index glasses lie in a band shifted toward lower Abbe numbers (the horizontal axis conventionally puts larger Abbe numbers on the left, so the band rises to the right). Glasses with lanthanum oxide and similar additions lie off this band, with a higher index at the same Abbe number. A higher index gives the same power with gentler curvature, which reduces spherical and other aberrations, so these glasses are common in camera lenses. Saying there is no relation, or that higher index means lower dispersion, misreads the trend.

optical-materials-026.question: A thin semiconductor film has a complex refractive index n + ik = 3.0 + 0.020i at a wavelength of 500 nm. Which value is closest to the depth at which the light intensity falls to 1/e (the inverse of the absorption coefficient α = 4πk/λ)?
choices: About 25 µm
About 4.0 µm
About 2.0 µm
optical-materials-026.explanation: The field amplitude decays as exp(−2πkz/λ) and the intensity as its square, so the absorption coefficient is α = 4πk/λ. α = 4π × 0.020/(500×10⁻⁷ cm) ≈ 5.0×10³ cm⁻¹, and the depth at which the intensity falls to 1/e is 1/α ≈ 2.0 µm. About 4.0 µm is λ/(2πk), the depth at which the amplitude falls to 1/e. About 25 µm leaves out the 4π and uses λ/k. Since k = 0.02 is tiny compared with n, the surface reflectance is set almost entirely by n: ((3.0 − 1)/(3.0 + 1))² = 25%. Even though k looks small, most of the light is absorbed within a few micrometers.

optical-materials-027.question: A metal has a complex refractive index n + ik = 0.50 + 3.0i at a certain wavelength. Which value is closest to the reflectance R = [(n − 1)² + k²]/[(n + 1)² + k²] for light at normal incidence from air?
choices: About 82%
About 11%
About 91%
optical-materials-027.explanation: (n − 1)² + k² = 0.25 + 9.0 = 9.25 and (n + 1)² + k² = 2.25 + 9.0 = 11.25, so R = 9.25/11.25 ≈ 0.82, about 82%. About 11% ignores k and uses the formula for a transparent material, ((n − 1)/(n + 1))², which cannot explain the high reflectance of metals. About 91% mistakes the magnitude of the amplitude reflection coefficient, √R, for the reflectance. A metal reflects strongly because its extinction coefficient k is large, and the larger k and the smaller n, the closer R gets to 1. The high reflectance of silver and aluminum comes from this. In a sufficiently thick metal no light is transmitted, and the remaining 1 − R, about 18% here, is absorbed near the surface.

optical-materials-028.question: A dielectric multilayer bandpass filter made by electron-beam evaporation is finished to its design specification in vacuum, but when it is taken out into air its center wavelength shifts slightly and also changes with humidity. Which combination of cause and remedy is correct?
choices: Oxygen in the air oxidizes the high-index layers and lowers their index, so the center wavelength shifts shorter. A protective metal layer on top prevents this
Atmospheric pressure bends the substrate and changes the layer thicknesses, so the center wavelength shifts shorter. A thicker substrate also removes the humidity dependence
Water enters the porous, columnar structure of the layers and raises their index, so the center wavelength shifts longer. Ion-assisted deposition or sputtering gives dense layers
optical-materials-028.explanation: Films evaporated onto a cool substrate tend to grow as columnar grains with many voids, and in air water molecules enter the voids. Replacing air (n ≈ 1) with water (n ≈ 1.33) raises the effective index of the layers and increases their optical thickness, so the center wavelength of the filter shifts to longer wavelengths, and it moves again as humidity and temperature change the amount of adsorbed water. The remedy is to make films with almost no voids, either by ion-assisted deposition, which bombards the growing film to densify it, or by sputtering or ion-beam sputtering. Oxidation or substrate bending cannot explain the humidity dependence. A metal protective layer would absorb light in a filter used in transmission.

optical-materials-029.question: Potassium bromide (KBr) crystals are often used for the windows and beamsplitter substrates of FTIR instruments. Which combination of property and handling precaution is correct for KBr?
choices: It transmits broadly from the visible to about 25 µm, but it dissolves in water, absorbs moisture and is soft, so it is handled in dry conditions and watched for fogging
It transmits broadly from the visible to about 25 µm in the mid-infrared, and it is hard and chemically stable, so it can be washed with water and used directly as an outdoor window
It transmits only to about 5 µm, beyond which lattice vibrations absorb, but it does not dissolve in water, so no care is needed when storing it in damp places
optical-materials-029.explanation: Alkali halide crystals such as KBr and NaCl have their lattice-vibration absorption at long wavelengths, so they transmit a wide range from the visible to the mid-infrared; KBr is usable to about 25 µm. As ionic crystals, however, they dissolve readily in water and absorb moisture from the air, which fogs the surface and lowers the transmittance. They are also soft and scratch easily, so they are stored in dry places such as a desiccator and not touched with bare hands. Outdoors or in damp environments, water-insoluble materials such as ZnSe are used instead. Transmission only to about 5 µm describes sapphire. CaF₂ also reaches only about 10 µm, so KBr is the material that covers the whole FTIR mid-infrared range in a single window.

optical-materials-030.question: After melting and solidifying, blocks of optical glass undergo precision annealing, in which they are cooled slowly over a long time from around the transformation temperature. Which statement about annealing and the cooling rate is correct?
choices: Annealing only removes internal stress; the cooling rate has no effect on the refractive index, so the index a manufacturer quotes does not depend on the annealing conditions
It reduces internal stress and index inhomogeneity, and slower cooling gives a higher index, so the annealing conditions are controlled to reach the target index
Faster cooling packs the structure more densely and raises the index, so glasses that need a high index are quenched quickly instead of being annealed
optical-materials-030.explanation: The cooling rate of a glass changes the temperature at which its structure freezes in (the fictive temperature). The slower it is cooled, the lower the temperature and the denser the structure that freezes in, and the refractive index becomes slightly higher. Optical glass manufacturers therefore anneal at a set cooling rate to bring the index of each melt to its specified value, and at the same time reduce the stress (birefringence) and index inhomogeneity caused by temperature differences within the block. Saying the annealing conditions do not affect the index is wrong; even the data-sheet index refers to a defined cooling rate. Rapid cooling freezes in a looser structure with a lower index and leaves large stresses. To build a lens to its design values, the measured index of each glass block is used.
